blocks.text: Do They Rely on Master Shandao?

inline.s: Question: Master Shandao, regarding
how the Pure Land school cultivates,
has clear instructions:

Now there are two kinds of practice: first, the correct practice; second, the miscellaneous practice. As for the correct practice: to practise in reliance on the rebirth scriptures is called the correct practice. What are these?
With single mind
recite this Sutra on Contemplation, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so forth;
with single mind
concentrate the thoughts, contemplating and recollecting the adornment of the two rewards of that land. If bowing, then
with single mind
bow exclusively to that Buddha; if reciting aloud, then
with single mind
recite exclusively that Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then
with single mind
praise and make offerings exclusively. This is called the correct practice. Again, within this correct practice there are two kinds: first,
with single mind
recite exclusively the name of Amitābha Buddha; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to the length of time, not letting go thought after thought, this is called
the karma of correct samādhi

, because it accords with the Buddha's vow. If one relies on bowing, reciting, and so forth, these are called the assisting practice. Apart from these correct and assisting practices, all other good deeds are called the miscellaneous practice. If one cultivates the aforementioned correct and assisting practices, with the mind constantly drawing near,
recollection never interrupted,
it is called unimpeded.”

Master Honen and his followers (Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and others) claim to rely on Master Shandao, so they should practise earnestly and truly according to this instruction. Not only do they not practise it,
they instead proclaim 'the moment faith arises, one attains rebirth'
(since the moment faith arises one attains rebirth, what need of the correct and assisting practices)
, and 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth'

(since reciting the name surely attains rebirth, what need of single mind? Moreover 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth' is diametrically opposed to Master Shandao's teachings 'being continuous, one is at once reborn' and 'right mindfulness at death')
and also 'the gate of the extensive vow'
(this is Honen twisting Master Shandao's teaching and forcing it onto him; see
Honen's Fabricated Gate of the Extensive Vow
article)
and other such sayings, which run completely counter to Master Shandao's instructions.
Since they do not truly believe in Master Shandao, why do they raise the banner of relying on him and call this Master Shandao's Pure Land thought?

Answer: Because if people knew these sayings were their own, being plainly contrary to the meaning of the scriptures, they would be met with contempt and no one would believe them. But if, by taking passages out of context, twisting Master Shandao's own text, and so on, they falsely claim this is Master Shandao's Pure Land thought, and then say: 'Since Master Shandao is the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha, his thought '
is as if spoken by Amitābha Buddha himself.'
Then they can deceive the believers, and no one dares to criticize or oppose. Nevertheless,
what is false is false; the disguise must be stripped away.

Master Shandao has three very important teachings: 'the correct and assisting practices,' 'being continuous, one is at once reborn,' and 'right mindfulness at death.' The 'sayings of Master Shandao' they compiled (see the Collected Works of Master Shandao, compiled by Master Huijing and Master Jingzong, published by the Pure Land Publishing House in 2005) they dare not include, fearing their true nature would be exposed. This fully proves that their reliance on Master Shandao is false,
and that under the banner of 'reliance' they peddle their own wares;
and it fully proves that the 'Master Shandao's Pure Land thought' they propagate is not the true Pure Land thought of Master Shandao,
but is constructed from their own wares.
Just watch the video Master Shandao's Pure Land Thought (lectured by Master Jingzong in 2006) and you will know.
Master Jingzong, in
Master Shandao's Pure Land Thought
lectures, says over and over that
the 'gate of the extensive vow' and 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth' are the core of Master Shandao's Pure Land thought. But what is the fact? The fact is:
Master Shandao never spoke of the gate of the extensive vow at all; this is entirely fabricated by Master Honen
(see
Honen's Fabricated Gate of the Extensive Vow
article)
. Master Shandao also never said that 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth.' On the contrary, Master Shandao said: 'being continuous, one is at once reborn'
(see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
article)

The 'gate of the extensive vow' and 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth' that they fabricated themselves, they force onto Master Shandao, falsely claiming this is Master Shandao's Pure Land thought. Is this how one propagates Master Shandao's Pure Land thought?
Now I shall transcribe these three very important teachings of Master Shandao:
“Now there are two kinds of practice: first, the correct practice; second, the miscellaneous practice.
As for the correct practice: to practise in reliance on the rebirth scriptures is called the correct practice. What are these?
With single mind
recite this Sutra on Contemplation, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so forth;
with single mind
concentrate the thoughts, contemplating and recollecting the adornment of the two rewards of that land. If bowing, then
with single mind
bow exclusively to that Buddha; if reciting aloud, then
with single mind
recite exclusively that Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then
with single mind
praise and make offerings exclusively. This is called the correct practice. Again, within this correct practice there are two kinds: first,
with single mind
recite exclusively the name of Amitābha Buddha; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to the length of time, not letting go thought after thought, this is called
the karma of correct samādhi

, because it accords with the Buddha's vow. If one relies on bowing, reciting, and so forth, these are called the assisting practice. Apart from these correct and assisting practices, all other good deeds are called the miscellaneous practice. If one cultivates the aforementioned correct and assisting practices, with the mind constantly drawing near,
recollection never interrupted,
it is called unimpeded.”
(The Four-Volume Commentary on the Sutra on Contemplation.)

blocks.text: 2. Being Continuous, One Is At Once Reborn

inline.s: “Question: Why does he not have one practise contemplation, but directly command exclusive recitation of the name? Answer: Because the hindrances of sentient beings are heavy, the objects of contemplation are subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness is agitated and the spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the great sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
in compassion, directly urges exclusive recitation of the name. Precisely because reciting the name is easy,
being continuous, one is at once reborn.
If one can
recite thought after thought without break
and so to the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why? Because there are no external distracting conditions, and
one attains right mindfulness;

because it accords with the Buddha's primal vow, because it does not violate the teaching, because it follows the Buddha's words. If one abandons exclusive recitation and cultivates miscellaneous karma, of a hundred one rarely gets one or two, of a thousand one rarely gets three or four. Why? Because mixed conditions stir things up, and
one loses right mindfulness;
because it does not accord with the Buddha's primal vow, because it violates the teaching, because it does not follow the Buddha's words,
because the binding of thought is not continuous,
because the mind is not continuously mindful of the Buddha's grace,

because though one does deeds of karma they are ever tied to fame and profit, because one delights in approaching mixed conditions, hindering oneself and hindering others' correct practice of rebirth. I wish all people to reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never give up,
when the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is already reborn,
forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood, how delightful!”
(The Essentials of the Teaching on the Whole and the Mixed Two Cultivations of Pure Karma by Master Shandao of Tang.)
“When one is gravely ill and about to die, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor make sounds of sighing and regret, disturbing the mind and spirit,
causing him to lose right mindfulness.
But all together with one voice recite the Buddha's name, and only after his breath is finished may they lament.
If he has the slightest thought of clinging to this world, it becomes an impediment, and he cannot gain liberation.
If one obtains a person who understands the Pure Land to come frequently and encourage him, this is extremely fortunate. If one follows this, he will certainly be reborn, without any doubt.

...This method, used by monks, lay people, and even those who have never recited the Buddha's name, all attain rebirth, without any doubt. I have often seen worldly people who in daily life recite the Buddha and praise, vowing to seek rebirth in the West, very earnest
(sincere and genuine).
But when it comes to illness, they again fear death, and never speak of the matter of rebirth and liberation. Only when their breath fades and life ends,
do their consciousness pass into the netherworld,
and only then do they begin the ten recitations. Just like shutting the door after the thief has gone, what use is it? Life and death are great matters;
one must make the effort oneself.
If one thought goes wrong, one suffers for aeons;
who can take one's place? Think on this! Think on this! When one has nothing to do, one should take this method
and practise it diligently
—this is
the great matter at death.
Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death and Rebirth
These three teachings of Master Shandao are a mirror that reveals monsters; compare the sayings of Honen and others against them, and whether they are true or false, right or wrong, is seen at once.
Question: Please explain these three very important teachings of Master Shandao.
Answer: Here is the explanation:

The following teaching, taken from the Four-Volume Commentary on the Sutra on Contemplation, is Master Shandao's important instruction on how the Pure Land school cultivates. Here Master Shandao lays great emphasis on single mind: whether reading the sutras, recollecting, bowing to the Buddha, upholding the Name, or praising and making offerings, one must be single-minded, for this is the key to correct practice! Single mind is focus without distraction.

Now there are two kinds of practice: first, the correct practice; second, the miscellaneous practice. As for the correct practice: to practise in reliance on the rebirth scriptures is called the correct practice. What are these? With single mind recite this Sutra on Contemplation, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so forth, with single mind concentrate the thoughts, contemplating and recollecting the adornment of the two rewards of that land. If bowing, then with single mind bow exclusively to that Buddha; if reciting aloud, then with single mind recite exclusively that Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then with single mind praise and make offerings exclusively. This is called the correct practice.

Now, there are two kinds of practice: first, the correct practice; second, the miscellaneous practice. The correct practice is to practise in reliance on the practices of the rebirth scriptures; this is the correct practice. Which are the correct practices? Single-mindedly and attentively reading the Sutra on Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so on; single-mindedly and attentively contemplating, observing, and recollecting the adornment of the two rewards of the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. If bowing to the Buddha, then single-mindedly and attentively bowing to Amitābha Buddha; if reciting aloud, then single-mindedly and attentively reciting Amitābha Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then single-mindedly and attentively praising and making offerings; only this is called the correct practice.

Wangsheng jing (the rebirth scriptures): namely the three Pure Land scriptures, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Sutra on Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitābha Sutra. Yan zhengxing zhe (as for the correct practice): here 'yan' is an initial particle with no meaning; for example, 'yan guiyu hao' means 'to return to harmony' (to be reconciled with each other again). Er bao (the two rewards): the primary reward and the dependent reward. The primary reward is the body, because the body, produced by the karmic cause, directly receives its retribution, hence called the primary reward. The dependent reward is the retribution in which the body dwells, such as the land, houses, utensils, and so on.

Again, within this correct practice there are two kinds: first, with single mind exclusively reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to the length of time, not letting go thought after thought, this is called the karma of correct samādhi, because it accords with the Buddha's vow; if one relies on bowing, reciting, and so forth, these are called the assisting practice. Apart from these correct and assisting practices, all other good deeds are called the miscellaneous practice. If one cultivates the aforementioned correct and assisting practices, with the mind constantly drawing near, recollection never interrupted, it is called unimpeded.

Again, within this correct practice there are two kinds: first, single-mindedly and attentively reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to the length of time, not letting go thought after thought, this is called the karma of correct samādhi, because it accords with Amitābha Buddha's great vow; if bowing, praising, making offerings, and so forth, these are called the assisting practice. Apart from these correct and assisting practices, all other good deeds are called the miscellaneous practice. If one cultivates these correct and assisting practices, with the mind constantly drawing near to Amitābha Buddha, recollection never interrupted, it is called unimpeded (without the admixture of false thoughts).

Zhengding (correct concentration): correct meditation. When body and mind are pure and clear, without being scattered, it is called 'correct concentration.' One of the eightfold noble path. Ba zheng dao (the eightfold noble path): also called the eight holy paths, that is, the eight ways of the sages. 1. Correct view: correct understanding. 2. Correct thought: correct thinking. 3. Correct speech: proper words. 4. Correct action: proper conduct. 5. Correct livelihood: proper occupation or living. 6. Correct effort: proper diligence. 7. Correct mindfulness: right recollection. 8. Correct concentration: correct meditation. The Amitābha Sutra says: 'These birds, in the six periods of day and night, utter harmonious and elegant sounds. Their voices expound the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of bodhi, the '
eight factors of the holy path,
and such dharmas.' Ye (karma): the action of body, speech, and mind.

blocks.text: 2. Being Continuous, One Is At Once Reborn

inline.s: The following teaching is taken from the Essentials of the Teaching on the Whole and the Mixed Two Cultivations of Pure Karma by Master Shandao of Tang.

Master Yinguang greatly praised this teaching, saying: 'Master Shandao is a manifestation of Amitābha; he has great spiritual power and great wisdom. In propagating the Pure Land, he does not esteem the mysterious and subtle, but only teaches people to cultivate at the sincere, real, and ordinary level.
As for the two cultivations, the whole and the mixed, he reveals their benefit is without limit.'
(The Collected Letters of Master Yinguang, reply to the brothers of a certain layman of Yongjia.)

Question: Why does he not have one practise contemplation, but directly command exclusive recitation of the name? Answer: Because the hindrances of sentient beings are heavy, the objects of contemplation are subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness is agitated and the spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the great sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)

in compassion, directly urges exclusive recitation of the name. Precisely because reciting the name is easy, being continuous, one is at once reborn. If one can recite thought after thought without break and so to the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why? Because there are no external distracting conditions, one attains right mindfulness; because it accords with the Buddha's primal vow, because it does not violate the teaching, because it follows the Buddha's words.

Question: Why did he not have one practise contemplation (referring to the thirteen contemplations in the Sutra on Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, such as the contemplation of the sun and of the water), but directly teach exclusive recitation of the name? Answer: Because the karmic hindrances of sentient beings are deep and heavy, the objects of contemplation (the objects contemplated) are subtle while the mind is coarse, the consciousness is agitated and the spirit flies, so practising contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore Śākyamuni Buddha, in compassion, directly teaches exclusive recitation of Amitābha Buddha's name. Precisely because reciting the name is easy, as long as the thought of recitation continues thought after thought, one at once attains rebirth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. If one's thought of recitation continues thought after thought, one who practises thus for one's whole life, of ten people ten are reborn, of a hundred a hundred are reborn. Why? Because exclusive recitation of the name means the mind does not reach outward (the mind does not cling to external objects), and thus one attains right mindfulness; because it accords with Amitābha Buddha's primal vow, because it does not violate Śākyamuni Buddha's teaching, because it follows Śākyamuni Buddha's holy words.

Xiangxu ji sheng (being continuous, one is at once reborn): 'being continuous, one is at once reborn' means that the thought of recitation continues thought after thought, and at the end of life one at once attains rebirth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. Here 'continuous' is the 'pure thought continuous' spoken of in the Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Reciting the Buddha by the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, that is, the thought of recitation continuing thought after thought, with no false thought mixed in the midst (if a false thought is mixed in, it is not continuity), and this is the state of single-minded, undistracted concentration (the state of the mind bound and not scattered). One must never misunderstand the two words 'continuous' here as the continuation of the name on the lips (while false thoughts are mixed in the mind). As the saying goes, a hair's breadth of error leads to a thousand leagues of mistake.

If one abandons exclusive recitation and cultivates miscellaneous karma, of a hundred one rarely gets one or two, of a thousand one rarely gets three or four. Why? Because mixed conditions stir things up and one loses right mindfulness; because it does not accord with the Buddha's primal vow, because it violates the teaching, because it does not follow the Buddha's words, because the binding of thought is not continuous, because the mind is not continuously mindful of the Buddha's grace, because though one does deeds of karma they are ever tied to fame and profit, because one delights in approaching mixed conditions, hindering oneself and hindering others' correct practice of rebirth.

If one abandons the single-minded, attentive recitation of Amitābha Buddha's name and cultivates miscellaneous karma, of a hundred people it is rare to find one or two reborn, of a thousand it is rare to find three or four reborn. Why? Because mixed conditions stir things up and one loses right mindfulness; because it does not accord with Amitābha Buddha's primal vow; because it violates Śākyamuni Buddha's teaching; because it does not follow Śākyamuni Buddha's holy words; because the binding of thought is not continuous; because the mind is not continuously mindful to repay the Buddha's grace; because though one does all kinds of karmic deeds, they are ever tied to fame and profit; because one delights in approaching mixed conditions, hindering oneself (obstructing oneself) and hindering others (obstructing others) in the correct practice of rebirth.

I wish all people to reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, day and night never give up; when the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is already reborn, forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood, how delightful!
I wish
all people
to reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
all
must rouse the mind and restrain themselves, day and night never giving up.
Practising thus,
when the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is born in
the Western Land of Utmost Bliss,
forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood, how delightful!

Qian nian mingzhong, hou nian ji sheng (when the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is at once reborn): this is to say that, because the recitation continues thought after thought, the very last thought at death is necessarily a thought of the Buddha's name, and
after that last thought
one is immediately reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.
The following teaching is taken from Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death and Rebirth. Whether rebirth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss requires right mindfulness at death,
this is the dividing line between the right and the wrong teachings of the Pure Land school.

The right teaching follows the meaning of the scriptures and affirms that right mindfulness at death is required; thus Master Shandao taught 'being continuous, one is at once reborn.' Master Yongming taught 'the ten recitations at death are accomplished.' Master Lianchi taught 'within, concentrate right mindfulness; without, move the Buddha to come welcome.' The wrong teaching, however, violates the meaning of the scriptures, denies that right mindfulness at death is required, and advocates 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth.'
Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death and Rebirth (for the full text see
Master Shandao's Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death and Rebirth

) causes the claim 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth' to collapse on its own; therefore the Collected Works of Master Shandao compiled by Master Huijing and Master Jingzong and published by the Pure Land Publishing House in
deleted this Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death and Rebirth.
From this one can see the intentions of Honen's followers! Tell me, is this how you rely on Master Shandao? Is this how you inherit and propagate Master Shandao's Pure Land thought?
Moreover, in the Four-Volume Commentary on the Sutra on Contemplation, Master Shandao explained the meaning of the chapter on the lowest rebirth, saying:

“'From this foolish person' down to 'the offenses of birth-and-death,' it clearly shows that hearing the Dharma and reciting the Buddha gets the present benefit, in ten points: first, it shows again the person who has done evil; second, it shows his life is extended but brief; third, it shows meeting a good friend at death; fourth, it shows the good person comforts and teaches him to recite the Buddha; fifth, it shows the suffering of death pressing the offender, leaving no way to recite the Buddha's name; sixth, it shows the good friend, knowing his suffering and his failing mindfulness, instead teaches him to recite aloud the name of Amitābha Buddha; seventh, it shows how many recitations, each sound unbroken; eighth, it shows the removal of offenses of many aeons; ninth,
it shows that right mindfulness at death means the golden lotus comes to respond;
tenth, it shows the speed of his going, straight to the land he is destined for.”
Please pay special attention: here Master Shandao says:
right mindfulness at death and rebirth
('it shows that right mindfulness at death means the golden lotus comes to respond'). (See
Commentary on the Chapter on the Lowest Rebirth in the Sutra on Contemplation
article.) Yet the Primal Vow school, which claims aloud to 'rely on Master Shandao,' resolutely opposes rebirth through right mindfulness at death!

When one is gravely ill and about to die, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor make sounds of sighing and regret, disturbing the mind and spirit and causing him to lose right mindfulness. But all together with one voice recite the Buddha's name, and only after his breath is finished may they lament. If he has the slightest thought of clinging to this world, it becomes an impediment, and he cannot gain liberation. If one obtains a person who understands the Pure Land to come frequently and encourage him, this is extremely fortunate. If one follows this, he will certainly be reborn, without any doubt.

If one is gravely ill and about to die, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor make sounds of sighing and regret, lest they disturb the mind and spirit of the patient and cause him to lose right mindfulness. Instead they must recite the Buddha's name in unison, and only after the patient's breath has ended may they lament. For if the patient has the slightest thought of clinging to this world, it becomes an impediment to his rebirth, and he cannot gain liberation. If one can have a person who understands the Pure Land come frequently to encourage him, this is a great blessing. If one acts according to this, the patient will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, without any doubt.

This method, used by monks, lay people, and even those who have never recited the Buddha's name, all attain rebirth, without any doubt. I have often seen worldly people who in daily life recite the Buddha and praise, vowing to seek rebirth in the West, very earnest
(sincere and genuine).

But when it comes to illness, they again fear death, and never speak of the matter of rebirth and liberation. Only when their breath fades and life ends, and their consciousness passes into the netherworld, do they begin the ten recitations. Just like shutting the door after the thief has gone, what use is it? Life and death are great matters; one must make the effort oneself. If one thought goes wrong, one suffers for aeons; who can take one's place? Think on this! Think on this! When one has nothing to do, one should take this method and practise it diligently, for this is the great matter at death.

This method of 'right mindfulness at death and rebirth' (the patient should try his utmost to maintain right mindfulness at death; the relatives must not weep and sigh lest they disturb the patient's right mindfulness at death; and the timely guidance and encouragement of a good friend can help the patient raise and maintain right mindfulness at death), used by monks, lay people, and even those who have never recited the Buddha's name, all attain rebirth, without any doubt. I have seen many people in the world who in daily life recite the Buddha and praise, vowing to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, very sincere and genuine. But when they fall ill, they again fear death and speak not at all of the matter of rebirth and liberation. Only when their own breath fades and life ends, and their consciousness enters the netherworld, do they begin to recite the Buddha in ten thoughts. This is exactly like shutting the door after the thief has gone (the thief has already stolen the goods before one shuts the door to guard against him), what use is it? Life and death are great matters; one must diligently apply oneself.
If one thought goes wrong, one suffers for aeons;
who can take one's place?
Think on this! Think on this!

Before one falls ill, one should take this method of 'right mindfulness at death and rebirth' and practise it diligently (one should make full preparation for right mindfulness at death, which is what Master Yongming called 'preparing the ferry beforehand'; at the same time warn the relatives not to weep and sigh at that time, and it is even better to have the deathbed help of a good friend), for this is the great matter at death!

blocks.text: The Characteristics of the Wrong Teaching

inline.s: Question: On the practice of the Pure Land school there are many conflicting claims; some even say that the true Pure Land requires no practice. Which is right and which is wrong, and how should one distinguish?

Answer: The claim that the Pure Land school requires no practice is quite wrong. At the end of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha earnestly said: 'You should believe and follow,
and practise according to the Dharma.'
In the Sutra Praising the Pure Land and Its Buddha's Reception, the Buddha again and again earnestly said: '
practise as it is spoken.'

As for how to distinguish whether the various claims about the practice of the Pure Land school are right or wrong, one should judge according to the principle of 'rely on the Dharma, not on the person.' What accords with the words and meaning of the scriptures is right; what is contrary is wrong. Grand talk that cites no scriptures is indeed untrustworthy; but even when one cites scriptures or the teachings of the patriarchs, one must also note whether it is taking passages out of context or twisting the scriptures or the patriarchs' original words (the example just given, 'Honen's fabrication of the gate of the extensive vow,' is one such case).

In general, the wrong teaching has the following characteristics. First: it does not cite the scriptures, but fabricates out of thin air and makes things up. Second: it winds around, going east and west, round and round, so that people cannot tell what is spoken by the Buddha and what is spoken by a person, and they take a fallacy for the truth. Third: when it cites the scriptures, it takes passages out of context and twists them. Fourth: it says such and such a sutra says thus and so, but does not attach the original text. If you carefully look up the original text, either you cannot find it at all in the sutra they mention, or the corresponding text has already been deliberately altered by them. Observe these characteristics carefully and you will find them.
The Sutra Praising the Pure Land and Its Buddha's Reception is the '
Dharma-gate received by all the Buddhas
praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, of course including Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. In it the Buddha said:

“Sariputra, in this West there are also the Tathagata of Immeasurable Life, the Tathagata of Immeasurable Aggregates, the Tathagata of Immeasurable Light, the Tathagata of Immeasurable Banner, the Tathagata of Great Freedom, the Tathagata of Great Light, the Tathagata of Flaming Light, the Tathagata of the Great Jewel Banner, the Tathagata of Emitting Light, and Buddhas such as these, like the sands of the Ganges, dwelling in their own Buddhalands in the West. Each displays the vast tongue, covering the whole three-thousand great-thousand world all around, and speaks true words: you sentient beings, all should faithfully receive this 'praise of the inconceivable merit of the Buddhaland, the '
Dharma-gate received by all the Buddhas

Therefore students of the Pure Land should practise respectfully according to the teaching; what accords with the words and meaning of this Sutra Praising the Pure Land and Its Buddha's Reception is right, and what is contrary is wrong.

blocks.text: The True Pure Land and the False Pure Land

inline.s: Question: Some now say that certain people are impure Pure Land and certain are false Pure Land, and that they alone are the true Pure Land. How should one judge?

Answer: The so-called 'impure Pure Land' is the language of people who are arrogant, praising themselves and disparaging others, so we do not adopt it. As for who is the true Pure Land and who is the false Pure Land, we let the facts speak and history bear witness (see
The Primal Vow School Is an Attachment-Buddha External Path
To Honen's followers (Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and others), we address a few plain words:

If you yourselves wish to revere Japan's Master Honen as the patriarch, that is your own affair; but you must not place Honen, who has not even attained single-mindedness, above the patriarchs of our country's Pure Land school who realized the pratyutpanna samādhi and the samādhi of reciting the Buddha,
and even slander them as impure, without lineage, and so on.
Be it known that
Master Yongming, the manifestation of Amitābha Buddha
came to our country earlier than the time when Japan's Master Honen
was born.

And he left behind the hundred-fascicle Record of the Mirror of the Source and the six-fascicle Collected All-Good Return of Myriad Good Deeds, giving a comprehensive exposition of the whole Buddha-Dharma (of course including the Pure Land); and to clarify the prejudices of certain people in the Chan and Pure Land schools, he wrote the famous Four Selections, in which he said:
“With Chan and with the Pure Land, like a tiger wearing horns, in this life a teacher of people, in the future a Buddha and patriarch.”
How can these patriarchs who had both Chan and Pure Land be slandered as 'impure Pure Land' and denied?!
Since Master Yongming is a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha
(Master Yongming's birthday, the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, is taken as Amitābha Buddha's birthday)

, his thought is as if spoken by Amitābha Buddha himself. The successive patriarchs of the Pure Land school after Master Yongming take the Record of the Mirror of the Source as their standard and follow it, so how can one say they 'had no lineage'? This is what is meant by the dwarf spitting at the sun.

[Pratyutpanna-samādhi (Banzhou samādhi)] Also called the samādhi of the Buddhas Standing Before One: it means that one who cultivates this samādhi and succeeds can see the Buddhas of the ten directions standing before him. In practice one neither sits nor lies down — from morning until night, and from night until daybreak, one either walks or stands, taking ninety days as one period, and single-mindedly recites the name of Amitābha Buddha. [The Four Selections] The text reads:

“With Chan but not the Pure Land, nine of ten will miss the way; when the shadowy state appears, in a flash they’re swept away. Without Chan but with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice, ten thousand go; once one beholds Amitābha, how could awakening be slow? With Chan and with the Pure Land, like a tiger wearing horns is he; a teacher of men in this life, a Buddha and patriarch in the next to be. Without Chan and without the Pure Land, the iron bed and the bronze pillar abide; through myriad kalpas and a thousand lives, there is no one at your side.” [Criterion (guīniè)] Refers to the gnomon and its shadow, and by extension a standard or a rule. [Gnomon (guībiǎo)] An ancient Chinese astronomical instrument: a rule (the guī) laid flat on a stone base, with an upright pole (the biǎo) set at each of its north and south ends. From the length of the sun’s shadow one can determine the solar terms and the length of the year.
Q: Please explain the Four Selections.
A: The Four Selections is extremely important.

Master Yinguang said: “Later, when Master Yongming came into the world riding upon his vow, in the body of an ancient Buddha, he made the teachings plain and wrote books to spread them abroad. And fearing that students would not be clear about the road ahead and would confuse what is beneficial with what is harmful, he strove with all his might to bring forth the verse of the Four Selections.
It may be called the guiding principle of the whole Tripiṭaka and a guide for those who have lost their way
. In its eighty characters it enables students
to awaken at once to the essential path that leaves birth-and-death and realizes nirvāṇa
. Such a grandmotherly heart for saving the world has never been seen through the ages.” (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Letter to Monk Ti’an of Daxingshan Temple). Master Yinguang also said: “
If one speaks of self-power and other-power, and of the difficulty and ease of Chan and the Pure Land, nothing sets it out more clearly and plainly than Master Yongming Yanshou’s Four Selections

. According to the Four Selections, those who have mastered neither Chan nor the teachings must of course recite the Buddha’s name; but even those who have mastered both should recite it all the more. Though one may have mastered them, if one has not realized them, one must still recite the Buddha’s name in order to be freed from birth-and-death — that is the true principle.
Master Yongming is a manifestation of Amitābha Buddha
, greatly compassionate, opening and transforming living beings.” (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Dharma Talks Given at the World Buddhist Lay Association)
The text of the Four Selections
With Chan but not the Pure Land, nine of ten will miss the way; when the shadowy state appears, in a flash they’re swept away.
Without Chan but with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice, ten thousand go; once one beholds Amitābha, how could awakening be slow?
With Chan and with the Pure Land, like a tiger wearing horns is he; a teacher of men in this life, a Buddha and patriarch in the next to be.
Without Chan and without the Pure Land, the iron bed and the bronze pillar abide; through myriad kalpas and a thousand lives, there is no one at your side.

[Liàojian] The distinguishing and choosing among meanings. [The Four Selections] Four such selections. [With Chan] Clarifying the mind and seeing one’s nature (thoroughly perceiving the inherent nature). [With the Pure Land] True faith and earnest vow, reciting the Buddha’s name to single-mindedness without confusion (uninterrupted mindfulness). [Without Chan] Not having clarified the mind and seen one’s nature. [Without the Pure Land] Not having accomplished “true faith and earnest vow, reciting the Buddha’s name to single-mindedness without confusion (uninterrupted mindfulness).”
Now I shall explain the Four Selections as follows:
[With Chan but not the Pure Land, nine of ten will miss the way; when the shadowy state appears, in a flash they’re swept away.]

If one investigates Chan and clarifies the mind and sees one’s nature but has not severed the delusions of view and thought (as is the case with nine out of ten of those who have awakened), then when the shadowy state appears at the end of life one immediately follows the karmic force to be reborn, without the slightest mastery over oneself. Yet because the awakening has already severed the delusion of view, one will not be reborn in an evil realm again.

[Nine of ten will miss the way] Among those who have clarified the mind and seen their nature, at least nine out of ten have not severed the delusions of view and thought; for them, to cultivate Chan alone is to take the wrong road, because they cannot escape the round of rebirth. [Cuō] Error, mistake. [Shadowy state] The state of the intermediate existence, that is, the state that manifests at the moment of death from the karmic forces of good and evil of this life and of kalpas past. The instant this state appears, in the blink of an eye one follows one’s most violent karmic force, whether good or evil, and goes to be reborn in a good or evil realm, without the least mastery over oneself. [In a flash] Suddenly; swiftly; in the blink of an eye.
[Without Chan but with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice, ten thousand go; once one beholds Amitābha, how could awakening be slow?]

Though one has not yet clarified the mind and seen one’s nature, if one has true faith and an earnest vow, reciting the Buddha’s name to single-mindedness without confusion, one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss with absolute certainty (of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go). Having reached the Western Pure Land and seen Amitābha Buddha, one accomplishes Buddhahood in that one lifetime — would one still worry about not clarifying the mind and seeing one’s nature?
[With Chan and with the Pure Land, like a tiger wearing horns is he; a teacher of men in this life, a Buddha and patriarch in the next to be.]

One who has already clarified the mind and seen one’s nature and who also has true faith and an earnest vow, reciting the Buddha’s name to single-mindedness without confusion, is in this life a teacher of men; at the end of life one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss in the highest grade of the highest rank, and accomplishes Buddhahood in that one lifetime.
[Without Chan and without the Pure Land, the iron bed and the bronze pillar abide; through myriad kalpas and a thousand lives, there is no one at your side.]

One has neither clarified the mind and seen one’s nature nor accomplished “true faith and earnest vow, reciting the Buddha’s name to single-mindedness without confusion.” If at the end of life one’s right mindfulness is not clear and distinct, one is drawn along by karmic force and reborn within the six realms. Because one has not severed the delusion of view, one will wander into the evil realms, and the time spent fallen into the hells (the iron bed and the bronze pillar) is the longest of all: through myriad kalpas and a thousand lives, there is no one to rely upon.
